title: Compare and order decimals to thousandths

lesson.title: Which Decimal Is Bigger? Line Them Up!

steps.say: You already know how to compare decimals like zero point four two and zero point three seven, all the way to hundredths. Today we take one small step further, to thousandths, so we can tell which of two three-digit decimals is bigger.

visual.caption: Zero point four seven two: 4 tenths, 7 hundredths, 2 thousandths

steps.say: Here is the trick, and it is the same one you already use. Start at the front, at the tenths, and compare one place at a time. Tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths. The very first place where the two numbers are different tells you the winner right away, and you can stop there.

Let's compare zero point four seven two and zero point four eight. Tenths: both have a four, so it is a tie. Move on. Hundredths: seven against eight. Eight is bigger, so zero point four eight wins. We never even needed the thousandths. Look at the number line: zero point four seven two sits just before zero point four eight.

visual.caption: Jumping from 0.472 up to 0.48 — the arrow points right, so 0.48 is bigger

steps.say: Now the mistake almost everybody makes. Zero point two five has more digits than zero point three, so it looks longer and looks bigger. But longer does not mean bigger! Check the tenths: two against three. Three wins immediately. Think of Canadian money: twenty-five cents is less than thirty cents. On the number line, zero point two five sits to the left of zero point three.

visual.caption: 0.25 is left of 0.3 — more digits does not mean more value

steps.say: One helping hand: you can add zeros to the end of a decimal without changing its value, so every number has the same number of digits. Zero point three becomes zero point three zero zero, and zero point two five becomes zero point two five zero. Now they are easy to line up and compare, digit by digit.
So remember: line them up and compare from the left, one place at a time. The number of digits never decides the winner.

visual.caption: From smallest to biggest, left to right

lesson.answer: Compare from the left — tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — and stop at the first place that differs. Longer is NOT bigger!

practice.question: At the Vancouver track meet, Maya threw a beanbag zero point six zero five metres past the line, and Sam threw his zero point six one metres past. Imagine a number line that starts at zero point six zero and ends at zero point six two. Draw it yourself, mark both throws, and tell me who threw farther.
practice.answer: Sam. Tenths are both 6, a tie. Hundredths: Maya has 0 and Sam has 1, so Sam is bigger. Written the same length, zero point six one zero is more than zero point six zero five, so Sam's mark sits to the right on the number line.
